title: Near-linear communication for exact maximum flow with local outputs
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), does there exist a randomized two-party protocol and constants \(K_a\ge1\), integer \(r_a\ge0\), such that for every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge capacities in \([0,n^a]\), whose edges are partitioned between Alice and Bob, the protocol computes an exact maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with success probability at least \(2/3\) and communicates at most
\[
 K_a n\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil^{r_a}
\]
bits on every execution? Each party must output the flow on its own edges. Interaction is unrestricted, and local computation, storage and local output are free; all transmitted bits are charged.
why: A dense flow may assign values to quadratically many edges, yet each participant already knows its own part of the graph. The question asks whether this local knowledge lets them coordinate an exact optimum while exchanging only about as many bits as there are vertices.
status_note: The checked 2025 and 2026 papers give subquadratic randomized communication protocols, with soft-O(n^(3/2)) bits when capacities are polynomially bounded. Their guarantees include determining the flow on each party’s own edges, but do not reach n*polylog(n) bits. The near-linear existence question remains unresolved in this bounded source check. A lower bound for communicating an entire flow to a party without its graph does not settle the local-output model here.

sentences: Alice and Bob hold disjoint parts of a directed graph and want an exact maximum flow between public terminals.
For every fixed polynomial bound on integer capacities, the target is a protocol using n times a fixed power of log n communicated bits.
Each party outputs the flow only on its own edges, using free local computation and storage, with joint success probability at least two thirds.
The bit bound is worst-case over inputs and randomness, while the number of interactive rounds is unrestricted.
The checked recent protocols use roughly n to the three-halves power bits; a complete Lean-checked near-linear protocol or refutation is required.

definitions:
The common vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and the distinct terminals \(s,t\in V\) are public. The graph is loopless and has at most one edge for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; both opposite directed edges may be present. Alice privately receives a list \(E_A\) of edges and their nonnegative integer capacities, and Bob receives \(E_B\) and its capacities. The promise is \(E_A\cap E_B=\varnothing\), and \(E=E_A\cup E_B\). The partition is arbitrary. Apart from their own edges and the public vertex/terminal data, neither party is initially given the other party’s edge set, its cardinality or its capacities. Missing edges have no flow variable. Zero-capacity edges and isolated vertices are allowed, and there is no connectivity promise.

Each local input is the explicit finite list of endpoint labels and capacities in binary; its storage and local reading cost are not communication. The exponent \(a\) is a fixed public parameter, not a number growing with \(n\). A separate protocol and constants may be used for each fixed \(a\), but must work uniformly over every \(n\), graph, capacity assignment and edge partition in that regime. The question does not replace the polynomial capacity bound by arbitrary real numbers whose encodings could hide uncharged information.

A feasible flow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) for every edge and
\[
 \sum_{(v,w)\in E} f_{(v,w)}-
 \sum_{(w,v)\in E} f_{(w,v)}=0
 \quad\text{for every }v\notin\{s,t\}.
\]
Its value is the net outflow at \(s\),
\[
 \operatorname{val}(f)=
 \sum_{(s,w)\in E}f_{(s,w)}-
 \sum_{(w,s)\in E}f_{(w,s)}.
\]
An exact maximum flow attains the largest such value among all feasible flows. The zero flow is always feasible, including when no directed terminal path exists. Edges entering \(s\) or leaving \(t\) are permitted and are accounted for by the net-flow definition. Integral capacities ensure that an integral optimum exists, but any exactly represented rational optimum is an acceptable output.

At termination Alice outputs a rational value \(f_e\) for each \(e\in E_A\), and Bob does so for each \(e\in E_B\). Rational numbers use finite signed-integer numerator and positive-integer denominator encodings. The two local outputs together must be one feasible optimal flow in the union graph. A party may compute its output from its private graph and the transcript, using unlimited local time and storage. Neither party is required to learn the other party’s edges or output values. Requiring both parties also to know the maximum-flow value would cost only \(O_a(\log n)\) additional bits after successful local outputs; it is not a substitute for them.

An admissible protocol consists of two fixed classical algorithms, for the chosen \(a\), that may use a shared sequence of independent fair random bits and private fair random bits, all independent of the input. Communication follows the standard bit-transcript model: each transmitted bit costs one, and message framing, lengths and termination signals must be encoded in charged bits or determined by the already shared transcript and public randomness. Silence, local running time and the choice of message length do not provide an additional uncharged channel. For each fixed public random tape, the speaking order is determined by the protocol and transcript. Messages may be interactive, with no separate limit on the number of rounds. There is no quantum communication, shared entanglement, oracle, input-dependent advice or prior correlation carrying information about the graph.

The algorithms must terminate on every input satisfying the promise and every random tape. All transmitted bits, in both directions and including preprocessing communication and failure cases, count toward the stated worst-case bound. Local computations and output lengths need not satisfy a time or space bound. For each fixed valid input and edge partition, probability at least \(2/3\), over all protocol randomness, must yield a jointly valid optimum. This is a simultaneous success guarantee for the whole flow, not a separate per-edge probability or average over random graphs. On failure the outputs may be invalid. A worst-case communication bound is required, not merely expected communication.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, including the protocol’s exact local-output correctness, per-instance success probability, termination and worst-case bit bound for every fixed capacity exponent. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation in this same model, ruling out all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and constants for at least one fixed polynomial-capacity regime.

Computing only the optimum value or a minimum cut is not sufficient for the selected output task. A result for approximate flows, undirected graphs alone, bounded interaction or a different output convention must not be treated as resolving it. An \(n\log^b n\) lower bound for one fixed \(b\) would still be compatible with the requested bound for a larger exponent. The question is a binary asymptotic existence claim; numerical tolerance does not relax flow feasibility or optimality.

source_formulation.text: Blikstad asks for the communication complexity of maximum flow when graph edges are split between Alice and Bob, with arbitrarily many interactive rounds, and singles out a near-linear-in-vertex-count protocol as a concrete target. The user chose that target for directed graphs with polynomially bounded integer capacities and flow output on each party’s own edges.
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of Dagstuhl Seminar 22461 report, §4.2, printed p. 58; capacity, error and local-output scope selected by the user on 17 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The seminar question distinguishes communication from sequential computation: a fast centralized maximum-flow algorithm need not have a cheap simulation when the two parties hold different edges. It also allows arbitrary interaction, so this is not a fixed-round lower-bound question.

The October 2025 protocol computes an exact integral maximum flow using soft-O(n^(3/2) log U) bits, where U bounds the integer capacities. For polynomial capacities this is a subquadratic bound, but still larger than the selected near-linear target.

The July 2026 theorem explicitly gives each participant the flow on its own edges. Its local decoding uses the participant’s input graph, explaining why a full flow can be produced with less communication than would be needed to transmit a stand-alone encoding of all its edge values.

The same paper provides a finite-bit implementation of its real-word analysis. Its abstract states soft-O(n^(3/2) log-squared W) communicated bits for min-cost flow, which includes maximum flow after the usual polynomially bounded reduction. Counting arbitrary real words as single bits would not justify this card’s target.

checked_sources: Read Blikstad’s §4.2, Communication Complexity of Max-Flow, in Dynamic Graph Algorithms, Dagstuhl Seminar 22461 (13–18 November 2022), report DOI 10.4230/DagRep.12.11.45, printed p. 58. The source explicitly partitions edges between two parties, permits arbitrary interaction and singles out near-linear communication. Its suggested interior-point bound is labeled unverified there; it is not cited here as a proved 2022 theorem.

Read Gholizadeh–Jiang, A Subquadratic Two-Party Communication Protocol for Minimum Cost Flow, arXiv:2510.03427v1, 3 October 2025: Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 in the introduction, communication model §2 p. 8, and §5.3 pp. 30–32 including the reduction and capacity-scaling argument. Theorem 1.3 gives a randomized maximum-flow bound of soft-O(n^(3/2)*log U) communicated bits. The source proves an integral flow guarantee, which also meets this card’s exact rational-flow output requirement. Checked that v1 is the current arXiv version.

Read van den Brand–Song–Weng, Computing Flows in Subquadratic Space, ICALP 2026 Article 46, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.46: abstract and introduction pp. 46:1–46:3, Theorem 2 p. 46:4 and the following bit-complexity paragraph p. 46:5. Verified publication 1 July 2026 and associated arXiv:2605.09547v1, 10 May 2026. The local-output theorem is exact, with finite-bit implementation; the abstract gives soft-O(n^(3/2)*log^2 W) bits. Local graph access during decoding is explicitly what avoids a full-flow output-encoding lower bound.
